questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Production Function' refers to.
questions.a: The production function maps each combination of inputs, labour and capital, to the largest output technically obtainable from it, so it always describes efficient production under a given state of technology.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Production Function'.
questions.a: Given technology, the function states the ceiling on output from any input mix - no more is possible from the same inputs.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Production Function', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: q = f(labour, capital)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Short Run and Long Run' refers to.
questions.a: The short run is any period in which at least one factor stays fixed and output can be raised only by varying the other factor; the long run is long enough for every factor to be varied, so no fixed factor remains.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Short Run and Long Run'.
questions.a: Run length is defined by factor flexibility, not by calendar days or months.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Short Run and Long Run', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: time_horizon = fixed_factor_present (short run) versus all_factors_variable (long run)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Isoquant' refers to.
questions.a: An isoquant collects every input combination of labour and capital that yields the same maximum output, acting as the producer's counterpart of the consumer's indifference curve; with positive marginal products it slopes downward.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Isoquant'.
questions.a: One curve, one output level: many labour-capital mixes can bake the same-sized cake.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Isoquant', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: isoquant = set_of(factor_combinations) yielding equal output

concepts.title: Total Product, Average Product and Marginal Product

questions.q: Compute average product and marginal product from a total product schedule. Use the method 'Total Product, Average Product and Marginal Product'. Work with: change_in_input = 40, change_in_total_product = 25, total_product = 20, units_of_variable_input = 75. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of marginal_product.
questions.a: 0.625 per cent

questions.q: Find the addition to output when one more worker is employed. Use the method 'Total Product, Average Product and Marginal Product'. Work with: change_in_input = 500, change_in_total_product = 5, total_product = 60, units_of_variable_input = 100. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of marginal_product.
questions.a: 0.01 per cent

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Total Product, Average Product and Marginal Product' refers to.
questions.a: Holding other inputs constant, total product links each amount of the variable input to the output obtained, average product spreads that output over the units of input, and marginal product is the extra output from one more unit of the input.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Total Product, Average Product and Marginal Product'.
questions.a: Total is the schedule, average is output per worker, and marginal is the addition from the latest worker.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Total Product, Average Product and Marginal Product', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: average_product = total_product / units_of_variable_input

concepts.title: Law of Variable Proportions (Diminishing Marginal Product)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Law of Variable Proportions (Diminishing Marginal Product)' refers to.
questions.a: As more units of one factor are added to fixed amounts of the others, its marginal product first rises, then falls; the rise reflects better factor proportions, the fall the crowding of the variable factor on the fixed one.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Law of Variable Proportions (Diminishing Marginal Product)'.
questions.a: Changing proportions first help, then hurt: too little labour wastes land, too much crowds it.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Law of Variable Proportions (Diminishing Marginal Product)', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: marginal_product_pattern = rise_then_fall as variable input increases

concepts.title: Shapes of TP, MP and AP Curves and their Mutual Relation

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Shapes of TP, MP and AP Curves and their Mutual Relation' refers to.
questions.a: Total product rises at an increasing then decreasing rate, while marginal and average product curves are inverse U-shaped; marginal product leads average product - average rises while marginal lies above it, falls once marginal drops below, and marginal cuts average at its peak.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Shapes of TP, MP and AP Curves and their Mutual Relation'.
questions.a: The average follows the marginal: whichever way the marginal sits relative to it decides the average's direction.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Shapes of TP, MP and AP Curves and their Mutual Relation', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: mp_above_ap implies ap rising; mp_below_ap implies ap falling

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Returns to Scale' refers to.
questions.a: Scaling all inputs by the same proportion t may raise output in the same proportion (constant returns), a larger proportion (increasing returns), or a smaller one (decreasing returns); for the Cobb-Douglas form the sum of the exponents decides which case holds.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Returns to Scale'.
questions.a: Doubling everything may exactly double output, more than double it, or less - and the exponent sum tells which.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Returns to Scale', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: returns_case = compare(f(t * inputs), t * f(inputs))

concepts.title: Cost Function: Total Fixed, Total Variable and Total Cost

questions.q: Using the method 'Cost Function: Total Fixed, Total Variable and Total Cost', work with: total_fixed_cost = 5000, total_variable_cost = 8000. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of total_cost.
questions.a: 13000 rupees

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Cost Function: Total Fixed, Total Variable and Total Cost' and work with: total_fixed_cost = 5000, total_variable_cost = 12000. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of total_cost.
questions.a: 17000 rupees

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Cost Function: Total Fixed, Total Variable and Total Cost' refers to.
questions.a: For each output the firm picks the cheapest input combination, and in the short run its cost splits into a fixed part that does not vary with output and a variable part that does, their sum being total cost.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Cost Function: Total Fixed, Total Variable and Total Cost'.
questions.a: Fixed cost is the price of standing ready; variable cost grows with every extra unit produced.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Cost Function: Total Fixed, Total Variable and Total Cost', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: total_cost = total_fixed_cost + total_variable_cost

concepts.title: Average Costs: SAC, AVC and AFC

questions.q: Using the method 'Average Costs: SAC, AVC and AFC', work with: output = 75, total_fixed_cost = 2500, total_variable_cost = 80000. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of short_run_average_cost.
questions.a: 1100 years

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Average Costs: SAC, AVC and AFC' and work with: output = 8, total_fixed_cost = 500, total_variable_cost = 5000. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of short_run_average_cost.
questions.a: 687.5 years

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Average Costs: SAC, AVC and AFC' refers to.
questions.a: Per-unit costs divide each total by output: short run average cost equals total cost over output, average variable cost equals variable cost over output, and average fixed cost equals fixed cost over output, with average cost exactly the sum of the other two.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Average Costs: SAC, AVC and AFC'.
questions.a: Every per-unit figure is its total spread over output, and the averages stack up to the full unit cost.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Average Costs: SAC, AVC and AFC', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: short_run_average_cost = average_variable_cost + average_fixed_cost

questions.q: Using the method 'Short Run Marginal Cost', work with: change_in_output = 400, change_in_total_cost = 8000. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of marginal_cost.
questions.a: 20 per cent

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Short Run Marginal Cost' and work with: change_in_output = 150, change_in_total_cost = 80000. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of marginal_cost.
questions.a: 533.3333 per cent

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Short Run Marginal Cost' refers to.
questions.a: Marginal cost is the addition to total cost from producing one more unit; since fixed cost cannot change in the short run, this addition is entirely the change in variable cost, and summing marginal costs up to any output rebuilds the total variable cost.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Short Run Marginal Cost'.
questions.a: The cost of one more unit is the step in total cost, and every step is variable cost in disguise.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Short Run Marginal Cost', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: marginal_cost = change_in_total_cost / change_in_output

concepts.title: Shapes of Short Run Cost Curves

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Shapes of Short Run Cost Curves' refers to.
questions.a: Fixed cost is a horizontal line and average fixed cost a rectangular hyperbola; variable-cost-driven curves are U-shaped - marginal, average variable and average cost all fall, bottom out and rise, and the marginal curve pierces each average curve from below exactly at its minimum.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Shapes of Short Run Cost Curves'.
questions.a: Averages chase the marginal, so the marginal curve crosses each average at its lowest point.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Shapes of Short Run Cost Curves', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: smc_below_avc implies avc falling; smc_above_avc implies avc rising

concepts.title: Long Run Costs and their Returns-to-Scale Link

questions.q: Using the method 'Long Run Costs and their Returns-to-Scale Link', work with: decreasing_over_irs = 45, flat_over_crs = 6, rising_over_drs = 80. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of lrac_shape.
questions.a: 131 rupees

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Long Run Costs and their Returns-to-Scale Link' and work with: decreasing_over_irs = 20, flat_over_crs = 20, rising_over_drs = 4. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of lrac_shape.
questions.a: 44 rupees

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Long Run Costs and their Returns-to-Scale Link' refers to.
questions.a: With every input variable there is no fixed cost, so long run average and marginal costs describe the same total; increasing returns pull average cost down, decreasing returns push it up, and constant returns hold it flat, giving both curves their U shape with marginal cutting average at its minimum.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Long Run Costs and their Returns-to-Scale Link'.
questions.a: The long run average cost curve is the returns-to-scale story told in rupees per unit.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Long Run Costs and their Returns-to-Scale Link', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: lrac_shape = decreasing_over_irs + flat_over_crs + rising_over_drs
